clinicalPearls: APS is an autoantibody-mediated acquired thrombophilia defined by recurrent arterial or venous thrombosis, microvascular manifestations, and/or pregnancy morbidity; it affects primarily young females (Harrison 22e p.2837).
APS may occur alone (primary) or in association with other autoimmune diseases, mainly SLE; about one-third of SLE patients carry aPL antibodies and 10-15% of those develop APS (Harrison 22e p.2837).

Diagnosis should be seriously considered with thrombosis, cerebrovascular accidents in individuals younger than 55 years, or pregnancy morbidity, particularly in the presence of livedo reticularis or thrombocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.2838).

The three classical laboratory antibodies are lupus anticoagulant (LA), anticardiolipin (aCL), and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I (anti-beta2GPI); higher-risk profiles include triple positivity, IgG isotype, moderate-to-high titers, and persistent positivity (Harrison 22e p.2838-2839).
Laboratory criteria require persistence: moderate (40-79 units) or high (>=80 units) aCL/anti-beta2GPI titers confirmed on two occasions 12 weeks apart (Harrison 22e p.2838-2839).

In patients receiving anticoagulation, LA test positivity should be interpreted with caution; when features are highly reminiscent of APS but classical aPL are absent, antiphosphatidylserine/prothrombin antibody testing may have a diagnostic role (Harrison 22e p.2837).

Deep venous thrombosis occurs primarily in the lower extremities and often causes pulmonary emboli; cerebral venous thrombosis may present with intracranial hypertension and focal deficits (Harrison 22e p.2837).
Arterial thrombosis most commonly affects cerebral arteries, manifesting as transient ischemic attack, stroke, migraine, or cognitive dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.2837).
Libman-Sacks endocarditis (small, usually <1 cm, organized platelet-fibrin valve vegetations) and valve thickening are characteristic cardiac manifestations (Harrison 22e p.2837).
Thrombocytopenia and autoimmune hemolytic anemia are the main hematologic manifestations of APS (Harrison 22e p.2837).

DOACs have recently been shown to increase the risk of arterial events, especially in patients with triple positivity or previous arterial thrombosis, and a meta-analysis found prior thrombosis type did not change this increased arterial risk versus VKAs (Harrison 22e p.2839).
harrison.pathophysiology: APS is an autoantibody-mediated acquired thrombophilia. The major autoantibodies target phospholipid-binding plasma proteins, chiefly beta2-glycoprotein I (beta2GPI, a 43-kDa apolipoprotein of 326 amino acids in five domains) and prothrombin; anti-domain I IgG is associated with increased thrombotic risk, while the antithrombotic function of beta2GPI depends on its fifth domain. Lupus anticoagulant is a separate group of antibodies against phospholipid-binding proteins that prolongs in vitro clotting time which is not corrected by adding normal plasma. Antibody induction is thought to begin with endothelial injury (from infections, oxidative stress, or major physical stress such as surgery or trauma) in a permissive genetic background (HLA associations), driving increased endothelial apoptosis, autoantigen presentation, and an autoimmune response. Binding of aPL to disrupted endothelium produces a proinflammatory, prothrombotic state with monocyte and platelet activation, adhesion molecules and proinflammatory cytokines, complement and neutrophil activation, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, and thrombus formation. Type I interferon pathway activation and an imbalance between type I and III interferons have recently been proposed as mechanisms of thrombosis and obstetric complications (Harrison 22e p.2837).
additionalDifferentials: Inherited or acquired thrombophilias including factor V Leiden and other causes
For catastrophic APS: thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic-uremic syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
nonInfectiousMimics: Other inherited or acquired thrombophilias (e.g., factor V Leiden)
Livedo reticularis from vascular-wall disease (atherosclerosis, polyarteritis nodosa, SLE, cryoglobulinemia, lymphomas) or vascular-lumen disease (myeloproliferative disorders, hypercholesterolemia)
additionalInvestigations: Lupus anticoagulant testing as a three-step procedure: screening with activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and dilute Russell viper venom test (DRVVT), mixing study, and confirmation
Anticardiolipin and anti-beta2GPI IgG/IgM antibodies by standardized ELISA
Antiphosphatidylserine/prothrombin antibodies when APS features are present without classical aPL
Repeat aPL testing 12 weeks apart to confirm persistence
Assessment per 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria (>=3 points from clinical domains and >=3 points from laboratory domains)

Renal biopsy for suspected aPL-nephropathy (thrombotic microangiopathy in acute phase; fibrous intima hyperplasia, fibrous/fibrocellular arteriolar occlusions, focal cortical atrophy in chronic phase)
Cardiac MRI or histology for suspected myocardial disease; imaging for adrenal hemorrhage; BAL or pathology for pulmonary hemorrhage
redFlags: Catastrophic APS (CAPS): a rare, life-threatening, rapidly progressive thromboembolic disease simultaneously involving three or more organs, typically with microvascular thrombosis developing in less than a week
Thrombotic microangiopathy (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with severe thrombocytopenia) as a typical CAPS finding
Cerebrovascular accident in an individual younger than 55 years
Acute limb ischemia or digital gangrene from peripheral arterial thrombosis
Budd-Chiari syndrome from hepatic vein thrombosis
Pulmonary embolism or pulmonary hypertension from pulmonary arterial thrombosis
harrison.prognosis: Thrombotic and obstetric event risk is closely tied to the underlying aPL profile, depending on antibody type (IgG high risk vs IgM low risk), number of antibodies (two or three classical autoantibodies confer higher risk than a single antibody), titer (moderate-high vs low), and persistence on repeated measurements. Catastrophic APS is life-threatening and rapidly progressive. APS antibodies increase with age, though it is questionable whether they induce thrombotic events in elderly individuals (Harrison 22e p.2837-2839).
pitfalls: Paradoxical pitfall: lupus anticoagulant prolongs in vitro clotting tests (e.g., aPTT) yet is associated with thrombosis in vivo, not bleeding; the prolongation is NOT corrected by mixing with normal plasma, distinguishing it from a factor deficiency.

aPTT has variable sensitivity to lupus anticoagulant depending on the reagent used; aPTT prolongation is not specific because factor deficiencies or other inhibitors also prolong it, so confirmation requires lack of correction on mixing and correction with added phospholipids (Harrison 22e p.~700).
In patients receiving anticoagulation, lupus anticoagulant positivity should be interpreted with caution.
Classification requires that clinical manifestations with other equally or more likely explanations than APS not be counted toward the criteria.
aPL antibodies are frequently transiently positive, so persistence must be confirmed (titers on two occasions 12 weeks apart) before attributing disease.
harrison.severityClassification: 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria require at least 3 points from clinical domains AND at least 3 points from laboratory domains. Clinical domains: (1) venous thromboembolism, (2) arterial thrombosis, (3) microvascular events, (4) obstetric complications, (5) cardiac valve disease, (6) hematologic manifestations. Laboratory domains: (1) lupus anticoagulant, (2) anticardiolipin, and/or (3) anti-beta2GPI antibodies at moderate (40-79 units) or high (>=80 units) titers on two occasions 12 weeks apart. Definite CAPS requires all four: thrombosis in >=3 organs/systems; development in less than a week; histologic small-vessel thrombosis in at least one organ; and aPL presence (probable CAPS when a combination is present) (Harrison 22e p.2838-2839).
